actions.name: External inspection of right eye via camera
actions.result: No conjunctival injection, no discharge, no corneal haze visible. Lids and lashes normal. Pupil appears round, no obvious afferent defect on gross observation.

actions.name: External inspection of left eye via camera
actions.result: Normal appearance, no redness, no discharge, pseudophakic appearance not applicable (no prior surgery this eye).

actions.name: Monocular visual acuity check, each eye, using home eye chart or phone app at set distance
actions.result: Right eye: 20/30 with glasses on, patient reports mild blur he attributes to his usual nearsightedness. Left eye: 20/25 with glasses on.

actions.name: Confrontation visual field screening by self-report (patient covers one eye, examiner moves finger/object on screen to four quadrants)
actions.result: Right eye: dense field cut in the lower-inner (inferonasal) quadrant - consistent with the patient's report of a shadow rising from the bottom, nose-side of his vision; this field defect localizes to the same supero-temporal retinal area implicated by his temporal-sided flashes (flashes arise from vitreoretinal traction at the break itself, which is supero-temporal, while the field defect reflects the inverted projection of retina inferior and nasal to that same break). Patient does not see the object in the inferonasal quadrant. Left eye: full field to confrontation.

actions.name: Amsler grid test, right eye, performed by patient at home using printed/screen grid
actions.result: Central grid lines appear straight and intact when patient fixes centrally with right eye; no distortion or missing central square reported, consistent with macula still attached, though peripheral shadow limits confidence in testing.

actions.name: Amsler grid test, left eye
actions.result: Lines straight and intact, no distortion.

actions.name: Pupillary light reaction, gross assessment via camera (swinging flashlight if patient has one)
actions.result: Pupils appear briskly reactive bilaterally on camera; subtle relative afferent pupillary defect cannot be reliably excluded by video.

actions.name: Review ocular history and surgical record
actions.result: Right eye: phacoemulsification with posterior chamber IOL two years ago, uncomplicated per operative note. History of high myopia approximately -8.00 D both eyes since childhood. No prior retinal tears or detachment on record.

actions.name: Review diabetes and systemic history
actions.result: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, diagnosed 6 years ago, last HbA1c 7.8% three months ago. No known proliferative diabetic retinopathy on last dilated exam 11 months ago (mild nonproliferative changes noted bilaterally).

actions.name: Review prior dilated eye exam note (11 months ago)
actions.result: Mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy OU, no macular edema, peripheral retina reportedly flat without holes or lattice degeneration on that exam; vitreous described as showing early syneresis.

actions.name: Risk stratification for retinal detachment based on history and remote exam findings
actions.result: High-risk presentation: acute photopsia and floaters with a new, persistent visual field defect ('curtain') in a highly myopic, pseudophakic eye. The inferonasal visual field defect and the temporal-sided flashes are both consistent with a single supero-temporal retinal break: flashes arise from vitreoretinal traction directly at the break (supero-temporal retina, which projects to the temporal visual field... actually corresponds to the area of traction itself, independent of the inversion rule), while the field defect reflects detached retina inferior and nasal to the break, which projects (inverted vertically and horizontally) to the inferonasal visual field. Macula appears spared on functional testing but this does not exclude extramacular detachment requiring urgent repair.

actions.name: Decision on urgency and disposition
actions.result: Same-day, in-person dilated fundus examination with scleral depression by ophthalmology/retina service recommended. This cannot be confirmed or excluded by telehealth alone. Patient instructed to go to the retina clinic or emergency eye service today.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Acute symptomatic posterior vitreous detachment with high suspicion for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, right eye (macula probably still attached) in a highly myopic, pseudophakic patient
differential: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment with retinal tear(s), likely macula-sparing given preserved central acuity and Amsler testing
Posterior vitreous detachment without retinal break (flashes/floaters alone, no field defect would be expected - less likely given field cut)
Vitreous hemorrhage (would usually cause more diffuse blur, not isolated curtain-shaped field defect, though can coexist with a tear)
Diabetic vitreous traction or tractional retinal detachment (less likely given acute onset and known mild nonproliferative retinopathy only)
Migraine with visual aura (does not explain persistent monocular field defect lasting hours)
keyFindings: Three days of new floaters and photopsia, right eye only

New inferonasal visual field shadow since this morning, with temporal flashes - both findings localize to a single supero-temporal retinal break (traction at the break produces flashes felt temporally; the detaching retina inferior/nasal to the break produces the inverted inferonasal field cut)
High myopia (~-8 D) and pseudophakia in that eye, both major retinal detachment risk factors
Central acuity relatively preserved (20/30) and Amsler grid intact, suggesting macula currently attached
No pain, no redness - typical for retinal detachment, helps distinguish from inflammatory/infectious red eye causes
Known mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, previously flat peripheral retina, now with new symptoms
plan: Advise patient this is an emergency requiring same-day in-person dilated examination with scleral depression by a retina specialist or eye emergency department - cannot be managed by drops or new glasses

Arrange urgent referral/handoff to retina service today, before the patient's work commitments, emphasizing time-sensitivity especially since macula currently appears attached (better visual prognosis if repaired before macula detaches)
Advise patient to minimize activities that could worsen detachment extension while awaiting exam (avoid heavy lifting/straining) but not to delay care for the wedding order

Document remote findings clearly (acuity, confrontation fields, Amsler) as baseline but explicitly state these do not substitute for dilated fundoscopy and cannot exclude a peripheral retinal break or detachment
Ensure patient has transportation/plan to be seen same day; confirm he understood the urgency in his own words before ending call
Do not prescribe eye drops or defer to new glasses as requested by patient; clarify this is not a refractive problem
redFlags: Sudden shower of floaters with flashes
Any decline in central acuity or new Amsler distortion would indicate macula-involving detachment, escalating urgency further
educationPoints: Classic triad of flashes, floaters, and a curtain-shaped field defect should trigger urgent same-day dilated exam regardless of pain/redness status
High myopia and pseudophakia are major, additive risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Preserved central vision and normal Amsler grid suggest the macula is still attached, which is prognostically important but does NOT lower the urgency of same-day evaluation
Telehealth visual acuity, confrontation fields, and Amsler testing are useful triage tools but cannot replace dilated fundoscopy with scleral depression for peripheral retinal breaks/detachment
Patients may minimize urgency due to competing life demands (e.g., work deadlines); clear, direct communication about vision-threatening risk is essential
Diabetic retinopathy history is a relevant comorbidity but should not anchor the differential away from retinal detachment when classic risk factors and symptoms are present

Visual field defects from a retinal break are inverted both vertically and horizontally relative to detached retina: an inferonasal field defect corresponds to detachment of supero-temporal retina. Photopsia (flashes), however, arises from vitreoretinal traction directly at the break itself, so flashes are felt on the same side as the break's retinal location (supero-temporal retina correlating with flashes perceived temporally) - flashes and field-defect location are therefore both consistent with the same break, but should not be mapped by the same inversion rule used for the field defect.

artifacts.title: Cataract Surgery Operative Note - Right Eye
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Rosen, Ophthalmology
artifacts.body:
Procedure: Phacoemulsification with posterior chamber intraocular lens implantation, right eye.
Indication: Visually significant nuclear sclerotic cataract, right eye, in setting of high myopia.
Findings: Uncomplicated procedure, posterior capsule intact, IOL well-centered in the bag.
Postoperative course: Unremarkable per follow-up visits at 1 day, 1 week, 1 month. Final visual acuity 20/25 right eye with correction.
Plan: Routine follow-up with comprehensive eye exams given high myopia; standard postoperative precautions reviewed and patient advised to report any new or unusual visual symptoms promptly.

artifacts.title: Comprehensive Dilated Eye Exam - 11 Months Ago
artifacts.author: Dr. L. Chen, Ophthalmology
artifacts.body:
Reason for visit: Annual diabetic eye exam.
Visual acuity: 20/25 OD, 20/25 OS with correction.
Refraction: OD -8.00 sphere, OS -8.25 sphere (longstanding high myopia).
Anterior segment: Pseudophakic OD, clear lens OS, no cells or flare.
Vitreous: Early syneresis bilaterally, no hemorrhage.
Retina: Mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy OU with scattered microaneurysms and dot-blot hemorrhages, no macular edema on exam. Peripheral retina flat 360 degrees OU, no holes, tears, or lattice degeneration identified with scleral depression.
Impression: Mild NPDR OU, no DME. High myopia, pseudophakic OD.
Plan: Return in 12 months or sooner if any new visual symptoms develop.

artifacts.title: Visual Acuity Trend, Right Eye, With Correction
Telehealth Triage Note - Today
artifacts.author: Ophthalmology Resident (self, in progress)
artifacts.body:
S: 57-year-old man with high myopia and pseudophakia OD (s/p uncomplicated cataract surgery 2 years ago), type 2 diabetes with known mild NPDR, presents via video with 3 days of new floaters and flashing lights OD (flashes noted temporally/laterally), and since this morning a shadow/curtain rising from the inferonasal visual field (patient-reported as 'bottom corner, nose side'). No pain, no redness. Able to read with central vision when covering fellow eye. Concerned about work deadline, asks about drops or new glasses.
O: Remote exam notable for right eye confrontation field defect in the inferonasal quadrant, visual acuity 20/30 OD (baseline 20/25), Amsler grid intact centrally OD. External exam unremarkable, no injection. Pupils grossly reactive on camera. Prior exam 11 months ago showed flat peripheral retina OU and mild NPDR without DME.
A: Acute flashes/floaters with a visual field defect pattern consistent with a single supero-temporal retinal break - the temporal flashes localize to the site of vitreoretinal traction itself, while the inferonasal field defect reflects the inverted projection of retina detaching inferior and nasal to that break - in a high-risk eye (high myopia, pseudophakic). Presumed rhegmatogenous retinal detachment until proven otherwise by dilated exam with scleral depression. Macula appears attached by functional testing but this cannot be confirmed remotely.
P: Same-day in-person dilated exam by retina service. Patient advised of urgency and sight-threatening nature; declined initial requests for drops/new glasses are not appropriate for this presentation. Will coordinate handoff and confirm patient has transportation/plan to be seen today.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states the shadow 'feels about the same' as this morning and has not noticed it getting worse
mismatches.recordEvidence: Confrontation visual field testing today demonstrates a dense, well-defined inferotemporal field cut - a formal objective measurement the patient has not actually performed on himself since this morning, so his subjective sense of stability is not confirmed by any real comparison data
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients often estimate symptom stability by casual self-observation rather than structured testing; clinicians should perform objective field/acuity testing at the visit rather than relying on the patient's impression that things are 'about the same,' since early detachment progression can be subtle and the patient has no true baseline to compare against from earlier today.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports his blood sugars are 'mostly okay, maybe a little high sometimes'
mismatches.recordEvidence: Lab report from 3 months ago shows HbA1c 7.8% (H, reference 4.0-5.6%) and fasting glucose 148 mg/dL (H, reference 70-99 mg/dL), indicating suboptimal glycemic control above target for a diabetic eye disease risk standpoint
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient self-assessment of 'mostly okay' glucose control may not match objective HbA1c data; this is relevant context for diabetic retinopathy risk counseling even though the acute issue today is the suspected retinal detachment, not diabetic eye disease - the resident should recognize the discrepancy without letting it distract from the emergency at hand.

objectives.text: Elicit and recognize the classic symptom triad of acute flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like visual field defect as indicating probable rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Identify major risk factors for retinal detachment in this patient (high myopia, pseudophakia) and connect them to the current presentation
Perform and interpret feasible remote functional tests (confrontation visual fields, monocular acuity, Amsler grid) to assess whether the macula is likely still attached

Correctly triage the case as a same-day ophthalmic emergency requiring in-person dilated exam with scleral depression, rather than offering drops or a refraction, recognizing the limits of telehealth examination
Identify a mismatch between the patient's subjective impression of symptom stability and the lack of objective comparison data, and between reported versus documented glycemic control
Address patient concerns about work obligations and cost barriers with empathy while firmly communicating the sight-threatening urgency and arranging a concrete same-day plan

patient.name: Yusuf Demir
patient.appearance: A trim, middle-aged man with graying hair and glasses pushed up on his forehead, dressed in a collared shirt with a measuring tape still draped around his neck. He is seated in a small, cluttered back-office at his tailor shop, bolts of fabric visible behind him, with a somewhat anxious but polite demeanor, occasionally glancing off-screen as if checking the time.

persona.personality: Polite, hardworking, soft-spoken, tends to minimize problems and wait things out rather than seek help immediately
persona.communicationStyle: Respectful and cooperative, answers questions directly but may downplay severity; appreciates clear, simple explanations and reassurance
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious underneath a calm exterior, worried about work deadline competing with health concern, relieved to have someone to talk to about it
persona.background: Immigrated from Turkey in his twenties, has run a small tailoring shop in Paterson, New Jersey for over 20 years, well known in the local community for wedding and formal wear alterations. Married, two adult children. Takes pride in his craftsmanship and reliability to clients.
speechExamples: I didn't want to make a big fuss, I thought maybe it would just go away.
It's like a curtain, you know, coming up from the bottom corner.
I have three suits due Saturday for a wedding, I really need my eyes for this.
Is there really no way to just get some drops today and go from there?
Thank you, doctor, I just want to make sure I don't lose my sight, that would be terrible for my work.

Missing his Saturday wedding alteration deadline if he has to go to the hospital today
Cost of an urgent specialist visit without advance notice
Whether he might lose vision permanently in that eye
Balancing work responsibilities against the recommendation to seek care immediately

scenario.studentBrief: You are the ophthalmology resident on telehealth triage call. Yusuf Demir, 57, is calling about new eye symptoms in his right eye. Review his chart before the call. He has a history of high myopia and cataract surgery in that eye, plus type 2 diabetes. Conduct a focused remote eye history and feasible video-based exam, then determine the urgency of his presentation and the appropriate disposition.
scenario.chiefComplaint: New floaters, flashing lights, and a shadow in vision affecting the right eye, over the past three days, worse this morning
scenario.openingLine: Hello doctor, thank you for seeing me. For a few days now I've been seeing a bunch of little specks floating in my right eye and some flashes of light at the side, and this morning I noticed like a dark curtain coming up from the bottom corner of my vision.
tasks: Take a focused history of the floaters, flashes, and visual field shadow, including onset, laterality, and any pain or redness
Review the chart for key risk factors and prior eye exam findings
Perform feasible remote visual function tests: monocular acuity, confrontation visual fields, and Amsler grid testing
Formulate an assessment of urgency and clearly communicate the appropriate next steps, addressing the patient's concerns
Document findings and plan in an ophthalmology SOAP note

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at his tailor shop office in Paterson, New Jersey, during a work break
profile.summary: A 57-year-old highly myopic, pseudophakic tailor with type 2 diabetes presents by telehealth with three days of new floaters and flashes and a new inferior visual field shadow in his right eye, classic for an acute retinal detachment with the macula likely still attached. The case teaches recognition of sight-threatening red flags, appropriate remote functional testing, and firm same-day escalation to in-person dilated exam despite competing social and financial pressures, while staying within the limits of what telehealth ophthalmology can assess.
profile.title: Acute Flashes, Floaters, and a Visual Field Curtain in a High-Risk Pseudophakic Eye
